extracted.intended_audience: experimental physicists and opticians (Royal Society readership); researchers studying optical phenomena of grooved surfaces
extracted.subtask_description: Design, perform, and report laboratory experiments investigating periodical colours produced by grooved surfaces (metallic and transparent), including measurements of angular dependence, material/refractive-index effects, reflected vs transmitted tints, and theoretical interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize grooved surface by m and n
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize the grooved surface by two quantities: m represents the breadth of each groove (the surface removed) and n represents the breadth of the intermediate space (the original surface left).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly define and use m and n throughout experiments; relate observed phenomena to these quantities (e.g., m+n or the number of grooves per given space). The paper uses this characterization as the basis for all subsequent description and analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relate prismatic versus ordinary image intensities to m and n
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the colourless image is formed by the original portions n while prismatic images are formed by the sides of the grooves m; varying m and n changes the relative intensities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate ocularly by increasing m and diminishing n until n nearly disappears (or vice versa) and observe the intensity shifts (prismatic images increase as ordinary image fades). Include experiments that systematically vary m and n to show inverse behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use number of grooves (m + n) to predict dispersion and distance of prismatic images
rubrics_metrics.description: The general phenomena of the prismatic images — their distance from the common image and the dispersion of their colours — depend entirely on the magnitude of m + n, i.e., the number of grooves and intervals occupying any given space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify groove density (grooves per inch) and report the correspondence between m+n and measured angular separations and dispersions; compare with known laws (e.g., Fraunhofer's determinations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Record angle-dependent obliteration (defalcation) of particular colours
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe and document unaccountable defalcation (obliteration) of particular colours that vary with the angle of incidence and may affect some prismatic images and not others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record symmetry and angle-dependence of missing/obliterated tints; treat such effects as non-accidental and analyse their systematic occurrence across specimens and incidence angles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ varied illumination geometries (rectangular aperture, convergent beams)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use apertures that give convergent beams (e.g., a long narrow rectangular aperture with 30°–40° convergence) to observe phenomena across a wide range of incidence angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary the luminous aperture geometry to reveal fringes and coloured behaviour that may not be visible with a small disc of light; report aperture, convergence, and geometry explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabulate number and orders of colours vs grooves per unit length
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically measure and present tables relating number of grooves per inch to the orders and portions of orders of colours developed (e.g., 500, 625, 1000 grooves/inch and the orders observed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide detailed tables mapping groove density to observed orders/tints and incidence-angle ranges (as done in multiple tables in the paper). This is central empirical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute diversity of effects primarily to n (original surface width)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether observed diversity of colour effects depends more on n than on m+n; the more the original surface is ploughed away (smaller n), the more brilliant the tints and the more numerous the orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments that keep m+n similar while varying n (or vice versa) to test this conclusion and report how brilliance and number of orders change with n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce specimens with extensive removal of original surface and document limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Create specimens in which the original surface is nearly wholly removed to observe resulting phenomena (e.g., increased number/orders of colours and shift to greater angles of incidence), noting practical limitations (tool breakage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully document specimen fabrication (tooling, failures like broken diamond points) and how nearly removing n affects maxima and limits of observed colours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure angles of obliteration across multiple prismatic orders
rubrics_metrics.description: For each prismatic order, measure the incidence angles at which violet and red rays (and intermediate colours) are obliterated — e.g., violet obliterated at 74°, red at 66° in the 1st spectrum, with systematic shifts for higher orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report numerical angle measurements for minima/obliterations across orders and correlate positions between ordinary and prismatic images (use figures/diagrams to show correspondence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use monochromatic (homogeneous) illumination to simplify analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the phenomena under homogeneous illumination (single-colour light) to simplify and reveal the new series of periodical minima (represented as minima rectangles across images).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform experiments in red and violet light, map shaded minima regions, and use monochromatic experiments to make the law of the phenomenon visually and analytically obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test influence of surrounding medium (air, water, oil) on angular positions
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover grooved surfaces with different fluids (air, water, oil of cassia) and measure how angular distances of black/obliterated spaces change; observed sines are inversely proportional to indices of refraction of the fluids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report fluid types, measured angular distances, and compute/compare sines vs known refractive indices to demonstrate inverse proportionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare phenomena across different materials (metallic and transparent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat impressions/experiments on different substances (e.g., steel, tin, realgar, isinglass, wax, gold, silver, calcareous spar) to study influence of refractive power and material properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present comparative tables showing angles/tints/orders for each material; note material-dependent shifts (e.g., isinglass producing minima at smaller angles) and discuss whether differences stem from refractive index or impression sharpness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and report sharpness/quality of impressions and groove edge condition
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess and report how rounding or loss of sharpness of groove edges (e.g., isinglass edges rounded when removed while soft) affects number of prismatic images and observed phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use microscopy to inspect groove sharpness; report when rounding reduces prismatic images to fewer orders (e.g., mother-of-pearl–like behaviour) and account for this when interpreting refractive-power effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure and compare reflected versus transmitted tints
rubrics_metrics.description: Record both reflected and transmitted colours from transparent impressions and compare their numbers, qualities, angular dependence, and non-complementarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide paired tables of reflected and transmitted tints at matched incidence angles; note differences in brightness behaviour with angle (transmitted tints increase brightness as incidence decreases while reflected tints become fainter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess temporal stability/aging of specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine preserved specimens over long intervals (years) to observe changes in colours, number of orders, and prismatic image visibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report long-term observations (e.g., specimens after six years showing changed orders or disappearance of colours) and note that colours remain same in all azimuths if incidence angle is constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify surface (polish/grind) to test dependence on n and groove sharpness
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberately alter the original plate surface by grinding/polishing to increase n and observe corresponding disappearance of ordinary-image colours, obliterated tints, and reduction/rounding of grooves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document modifications (amount of polishing), resulting changes in n and groove edges, and consequent loss or change of phenomena; use as a control to link surface condition to optical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct optical-contact and thickness-dependence experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Place an impressed film in optical contact with glass of varying thickness and observe fringes across reflected images; fringe breadth diminishes as glass thickness increases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report glass thicknesses and orientation, illustrate fringe spacing relative to prismatic images, and use such experiments to tie fringe production to interference effects and specimen–substrate relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test and rule out competing explanations (diffraction from narrow slits) empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether phenomena are due to diffraction/interference from the spaces n considered as narrow slits by testing for dependence on distance of luminous object and observer and the expected geometry of bands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If colours/bands are unaffected by object or eye distance and do not form bands parallel to grooves, use this to rule out slit-diffraction explanations; explicitly test observer/object distance dependence as an anti-pattern check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use polarized light and theoretical analogies to probe mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare with experiments on complementary colours by metallic reflection of polarized light; consider the model of equivalent film thickness and whether two interfering pencils (one delayed) cause the colours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design polarized-light experiments and use them to distinguish whether interference arises from reflections within a sphere of reflecting activity or from a pencil that penetrates metal before reflection. Discuss theoretical implications and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary refractive-index contrast to extrapolate phenomenon limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Use fluids of increasing refractive power to show that diminishing the refractive power of intermediate spaces (by removing metal or applying high-index fluids) develops colours and can, in principle, lead to periodical colours without grooves when fluid index approaches that of metal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically apply fluids with different refractive indices and report tints/orders developed. Extrapolate cautiously, noting practical and theoretical limits (prediction that very high-index fluids could reproduce phenomena without grooves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspect groove microstructure for composite grooves as source of effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine grooves under microscope to detect when a nominally single groove m actually consists of two or more smaller reflecting spaces that can produce periodical colours even if m and n are large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use microscopic inspection to identify sub-structure in grooves and report when apparent large m actually contains finer periodic structure; interpret optical results accordingly rather than attributing them solely to m and n at the macroscopic scale.
